name: The 'noble lie' (myth of the metals)
plain_explanation: Plato proposes that the rulers deliberately teach citizens a myth -- that God made some people of gold (fit to rule), some of silver (fit to be soldiers), and the rest of bronze and iron (fit for manual labor) -- to make the class system feel natural and God-given.
precise_definition: A government-sanctioned foundational myth (the 'one royal lie'), asserting citizens are born of different divinely ordained metals corresponding to their social class, intended to be believed by nearly the entire population (rulers possibly excepted) and sustained across generations through education.
why_it_mattered: It makes explicit that Plato's ideal state requires systematic falsehood administered by the state 'as a prerogative of the government, just as giving medicine is of physicians,' which Russell singles out as incompatible with the spirit of philosophy itself.
historical_origin: Presented by Plato as a deliberately constructed civic myth, not an inherited religious tradition.
examples: Russell compares its plausibility to the historically real Japanese doctrine that the Mikado descended from the sun-goddess, noting professors were dismissed for questioning it.
objections: Russell: 'Plato does not seem to realize that the compulsory acceptance of such myths is incompatible with philosophy, and involves a kind of education which stunts intelligence.'
connection_to_politics_or_religion: The myth functions as a civic religion, deliberately engineered rather than organically inherited.
